> **The problem, in Cody's words:** his vegetables come out **charred on the outside and underdone in the middle**, and his first instinct was that the oven must be too hot — hence the 375°F question this entry carried. **He talked himself out of it mid-answer, and he landed in the right place:** ***"maybe I should have just cut thinner vegetables, quite frankly — that's probably what I should have done. So it can stay at 400, and then we specify how thick the vegetable should be."***
>
> **He's right, and here's why it isn't a temperature problem.** **The char is the point of this recipe** — that's the *Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat* idea the 400°F comes from in the first place, and it's what [§T39 Maillard vs. Caramelization](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md) is about. **Dropping the oven doesn't fix a raw middle; it just takes the char away too** — you'd be trading the good half of the result for the bad half. The actual variable is the distance from the surface to the center. **A thinner cut cooks through in the same time it takes the outside to char.** That's the whole trick, and it's what [§T32](t32-how-to-use-heat.md) calls the grilled-cheese test: *the outside should finish browning at the exact moment the inside finishes cooking.* When those two don't line up, the thing to change is the size of what you cut, not the number on the dial.
>
> **So: 400°F stays, and the recipe gains a thickness spec — see step 2.** The 375°F question is retired as **asked and declined**, by Cody, not by the cookbook.

**🟢 Easy** · **Prep ~10 min** · **Cook ~20–25 min** *(at 400°F, and pull them when they look right rather than when the timer says so)* · **Start to finish ~35 min**

**⏰ Countdown to dinner:** T−35 min oven to 400°F, elevated rack on the sheet pan; cut everything ½ to ¾ in., all the same size · T−25 min olive oil, rosemary sprigs, Tony's; onto the rack in one layer — 20 to 25 min (asparagus and thin things 12–15) · T−13 min check and turn the pan · T−0 pull them before they burn — firm, with color.

#### A. Ingredients

- Vegetables for roasting — **wing it**. ✅ *Cody's own list, 2026-09-09: **squash, zucchini, Brussels sprouts, carrots, asparagus** — that parenthetical is on the [Meal Planning Sheet](../meal-planning-sheet.md) line too.* Asparagus is called out by name on a second card as one that works well this way; **[§5.15 Roasted Asparagus](515-roasted-asparagus.md) is the asparagus-only version of this idea** (Canal House, with balsamic), and [§5.7 Brussels Sprouts](57-brussels-sprouts.md) ❤️ is his skillet method for the sprouts if you'd rather not roast them.
- Olive oil
- Tony's Cajun seasoning
- **Fresh rosemary** — a few sprigs *(Cody's addition, not on the card)*

#### B. Cooking Instructions

**1. Heat the oven to 400°F, and set an elevated rack on the sheet pan.**
**400°F is *Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat*'s number**, and it's the temperature Cody roasts at. **Then the part that actually changes how these come out: put a rack — a cooling rack, a grid, any elevated grate that fits — down on the cookie sheet, and roast on top of that instead of directly on the pan.** ✅ *Cody's own practice, 2026-09-08.* The reason is worth understanding because it is the whole difference between roasting and steaming: a vegetable sitting flat on a sheet pan gives off water, that water pools underneath it, and the underside sits and **steams** in its own moisture while the top browns. Lift it onto a rack and the hot air gets **all the way around** — the moisture drops away, every surface is dry, and every surface browns. It's the same principle [§T39 Maillard vs. Caramelization — GBD](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md) makes about giving vegetables room on the pan: **browning needs a dry surface and moving air**, and crowding or contact denies it both. The rack solves the contact half; not piling the pan solves the other half.

**2. Cut the vegetables ½ to ¾ inch thick — and cut them all the same size. This is the step that decides whether they cook through.**
✅ **Added 2026-09-08 as the answer to Cody's charred-outside/underdone-inside problem** — his own diagnosis was that he should have cut thinner vegetables, and this is that instruction written down. **Half an inch is the working number; three-quarters is the ceiling.** Cut a dense vegetable thicker than that at 400°F and the outside is black before the middle is done, which is exactly the failure he described.

*⚙️ **The thickness figures are cookbook judgment; the diagnosis is Cody's.** Sources, per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md): **Samin Nosrat's *Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat*** — already the source of this recipe's 400°F — makes 400°F the default for roasting vegetables and says plainly that **the right temperature shifts with the size and density of what you cut** and how loaded the tray is, which is the same relationship from the other direction; **America's Test Kitchen's "How to Roast Any Vegetable"**, for the practical band and for the rule that pieces be cut equal in size and spread in a single layer; and this book's own **[§T47](t47-cooking-vegetables-and-fruits--and-reverse-searing-them-too.md)** (Meathead), which says to cut root vegetables into smaller disks or chunks to speed them along and get more surface for browning, and to **err on the side of undercooking**. **Cody's own figures supersede these the day he cooks a pan and gives them.***

**Practical cut sizes, by what's actually on the pan:**

- **Dense root vegetables — carrots, parsnips, sweet potatoes, beets, turnips.** These are the ones that fail. **½-inch coins, or halved and quartered lengthwise into ½-inch batons.** A whole carrot roasted round is the classic charred-outside/raw-inside cut.
- **Potatoes.** **¾-inch chunks**, or halved if they're small new potatoes. Cut side down on the rack for the best face.
- **Onions.** **Wedges through the root end**, about ¾ inch at the thick edge — the root holds the layers together so they don't scatter.
- **Broccoli and cauliflower.** **Florets about 1½ inches across, with the stem trimmed to ½ inch.** These are mostly air, so they're allowed to be bigger than a root vegetable; it's the stem that has to be thin.
- **Brussels sprouts.** **Halved through the stem**, quartered if they're big ones. Never whole.
- **Zucchini, summer squash, eggplant, bell pepper.** **¾-inch pieces**, and expect them earlier than everything else.
- **Asparagus — the one the second card names.** **Whole spears, untrimmed except for the woody ends.** It's already thin, which is precisely why it works so well on this formula and why it comes off at the short end of the timing.

**Two rules that matter more than any of the numbers:** **cut everything on the pan to the same size**, because a mixed pan finishes at the speed of its thickest piece and burns at the speed of its thinnest; and **don't cut smaller than ½ inch** — vegetables shrink substantially in a hot oven, and pieces cut too small cook through before they have time to take any color at all, which is the opposite failure and just as disappointing. **If you want vegetables of genuinely different densities on one pan, cut the dense ones thinner rather than putting them all on at once.**

**3. Drizzle with olive oil, lay rosemary sprigs over the top, and season.**
Vegetables onto the rack, a **drizzle of olive oil** over them — enough to coat, not enough to pool — then **a few sprigs of fresh rosemary** laid over the top *(Cody's, not the card's)*, and **Tony's Cajun seasoning** to season. Spread them out in one layer with space between; a heaped pan steams no matter what rack it's sitting on.

**4. Roast at 400°F, 20 to 25 minutes — and pull them before they burn.**
Thinner things move faster: asparagus and other slender vegetables can be done closer to **12 to 15 minutes**, while dense root vegetables want the long end or a little past it. **Watch the pan, not the clock**, and take them out when they've got color on them and are still holding their shape. Check on them around the 12-minute mark and turn the pan — ovens have hot corners, and *Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat* says to rotate rather than trust the box to be even. **Cody's vegetables come out firm, and that's cause and effect rather than an accident — he pulls them before they burn.** ✅ *2026-09-08, in his own words.* That's a real tradeoff, honestly stated: leaving them in longer gets you softer and browner right up until it gets you burnt, and he'd rather eat them firm than risk the other end.

**If they're charring outside and still hard in the middle, go back to step 2 — that's a knife problem, not an oven problem.** ✅ *2026-09-08, Cody's own conclusion: the oven stays at 400°F and you cut thinner.* The char is what this recipe is for; a lower oven would take it away without fixing the middle. See the callout at the top of the entry.

#### Nutrition *(not calculable as written)*

This is a "wing it" formula with no fixed vegetables or amounts, so there's no single dish to compute exact numbers for. As a rough sense of scale, a 1-cup serving of most vegetables roasted in a light coating of olive oil runs somewhere around 120–180 calories, 8–12 g fat, 2–4 g protein, 12–18 g carbs, and 3–5 g fiber — but the real numbers swing with which vegetables go on the pan and how much oil gets used. The rosemary contributes nothing worth counting.

**What a serving is:** not fixed — whatever portion comes off the sheet pan.
